name: David Rahman

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, David. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you tell me stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Sure. I buy fresh fruit and vegetables for a food distributor called Northgate Foods, which supplies restaurants, care homes and about forty school kitchens. My day starts at six with the growers on the phone, finding out what's been picked, what got hit by rain, and who can do me a decent price on carrots this week. Then I build the orders on a big spreadsheet I've used for nine years, and by ten the trucks are being loaded off my numbers.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the growers. I've known Marek at the apple farm for eleven years, and when his frost wiped out half a crop, I found him other buyers instead of just dropping him. What wears me out is the head office pushing for cheaper and cheaper, and the new ordering portal they keep asking me to try, which I mostly avoid. I'm not a gadget person, never have been.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so, honestly. Half the people at head office have been talking about AI like it's going to run the place, and I'd enjoy a quiet laugh in the canteen. Online I'd probably say nothing, I don't post much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it'd be a relief. My job is all phone calls, gut feel and knowing which grower is telling the truth about his lettuce. If the computers only tidy up some paperwork, I keep doing what I'm good at and nobody asks me to change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing new, really. I'd keep my spreadsheet, keep ringing Marek and the others at six, and maybe finally let Hana, our admin, show me how the portal saves me twenty minutes on invoices. We'd keep putting a bit aside each month like we already do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Like a storm warning that turns out to be a bit of drizzle.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd let Hana show you the portal. Would you really?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably, if it's only invoices and nobody's watching me fumble it. I'd want her to write the steps on a sticky note. I'm not proud about it, but I'm not going to pretend I'm quick with new screens either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything about this picture that would still bother you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only that head office would use the hype as an excuse anyway. Head office doesn't need a clever computer to squeeze the growers. Head office already does that with a calculator. If nothing changes, the fight over fair prices is still there on Monday morning.

S0.say: I'd tell people at work that I told them so, and enjoy a quiet laugh in the canteen. Online I'd stay quiet because I hardly post anything.
S0.think: It would be a relief, because my job runs on phone calls, gut feel and knowing which grower is honest. If AI only tidies the paperwork, I keep doing what I'm good at.
S0.do: Keeps his six o'clock grower calls and his nine-year-old ordering spreadsheet. Lets the admin, Hana, show him the invoice portal if it saves twenty minutes, and keeps saving the usual amount each month.
S0.feel: Calm and a bit smug, like a storm warning that turned into drizzle.
S0.quote: Head office doesn't need a clever computer to squeeze the growers. Head office already does that with a calculator.
S0.fieldNote: David's identity rests on his grower relationships, especially Marek at the apple farm. His resistance to new tools is open and slightly embarrassed. Even in the calm picture his real grievance is with head office pushing prices down, not with technology.

steps.text: Keep the six o'clock grower calls and the ordering spreadsheet
Let Hana show him the invoice portal if it saves time

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say we need to be careful who gets squeezed out, and I'd mean the growers as much as us. With friends I'd say the companies will use this to cut staff, same as they always do. I'd probably share a post from the union about it, which is a big step for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be scared. My whole job is forecasting how much broccoli forty school kitchens need and phoning around for prices, and that's exactly the stuff a computer is good at. Priya in our office already uses something to draft supplier emails, and I've watched a colleague with an AI tool do in an hour what takes me a whole morning on the phones and the spreadsheet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First thing, I'd join the union properly instead of just paying the odd subscription. I'd push for a written agreement that nobody gets let go without retraining offered first. At home, Leila and I would stop the plan to redo the kitchen and keep that eight thousand in the bank, because we've only got about four months saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tight in the chest. I'm 43 with a mortgage and two kids, and I'm the slow one with computers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you're the slow one with computers. Would you try to learn the tools, or not?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd try the bare minimum, if the union got the company to pay for proper training in work hours. I'm not going to sit up at night with a chatbot. I know that sounds stubborn, and Leila tells me it is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your kids about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My son Zain is twelve and already asks why I write orders on paper first. I'd tell him the honest thing: Dad's job might change and I'm not good at change, but we'll be fine because your mother's a nurse and nurses don't get replaced by a laptop. I hope that's true.

S1.say: I'd say at work that we need to watch who gets squeezed out, growers included. I'd tell friends the companies will use AI to cut staff, and I'd share a union post about it.
S1.think: I'd be scared, because forecasting orders and phoning for prices is exactly what a computer does well. I've already watched a colleague do in an hour what takes me a morning.
S1.do: Joins the union properly and pushes for a written promise of retraining before any job cuts. Cancels the planned eight-thousand kitchen renovation to keep about four months of savings intact, and does only the training the company pays for in work hours.
S1.feel: Tight in the chest and exposed, as the slowest person with computers in a job made of computer-friendly tasks.
S1.quote: I've watched a colleague with an AI tool do in an hour what takes me a whole morning on the phones and the spreadsheet.
S1.fieldNote: David can describe his own exposure precisely, which makes his refusal to learn more striking. His instinct is collective rather than personal: protection through the union, not reskilling at night. The calm about his partner's nursing job is doing a lot of work for him.

steps.text: Join the union properly and push for a retraining-first agreement
Cancel the eight-thousand kitchen renovation and keep the cash

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it out loud: this is a disaster being done to people, not something that just happens. I'd be the one at the staff meeting asking what the plan is for the twelve of us in purchasing. Online I'd sign every petition going for a pause or a tax on these companies.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think I'd be out of work inside a year of it arriving. If the AI can talk to growers, read the weather and build forty school orders by itself, Northgate doesn't need a buyer at all, maybe one person to check it. And there's no robot bit of my job to hide in, because I don't lift anything except a phone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Straight away I'd cut everything that isn't the mortgage, food and the kids, so the gym, the second car and the summer trip go. I'd go to every union meeting and write to our MP about income support. I've thought about the warehouse floor, because robots come three years after, but that's three years at warehouse pay, and then they come for that too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick. I keep doing the sums and they don't work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the three years before robots. Does that gap mean anything for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The lads loading my delivery trucks would keep their jobs longer than I keep mine as the buyer, and I'd be asking the warehouse manager for a forklift slot. His name's Tony, he's a decent guy. I'd hate it, my back's not great, but three years of wages is three years of mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which bill goes unpaid first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably the credit card, then we'd ring the bank about the mortgage. Four months of savings goes in four months, there's no magic. I'd have to ask my brother for help, and I've never asked him for anything.

S2.say: I'd say this is a disaster being done to people, and I'd ask at the staff meeting what the plan is for purchasing. Online I'd sign every petition for a pause or a tax on the AI companies.
S2.think: I think I'd be out of work within a year, because nothing in my job needs hands. The people loading my trucks would keep their jobs longer than I keep mine.
S2.do: Cuts the gym, the second car and the summer trip at once, and goes to every union meeting while writing to his MP about income support. Asks the warehouse manager, Tony, about a forklift job to cover the three years before robots arrive.
S2.feel: Sick and out of options; the sums don't work and four months of savings won't stretch.
S2.quote: The lads loading my delivery trucks would keep their jobs longer than I keep mine as the buyer, and I'd be asking the warehouse manager for a forklift slot.
S2.fieldNote: This is where David breaks: high exposure, resistance to tools and only four months saved leave him with no plan he believes in. He sees the robot lag only as a short-term shelter in someone else's job. Asking his brother for help would cost him pride, which tells you how cornered he feels.

steps.text: Sell the second car and drop the gym and summer trip
Attend every union meeting and write to the MP about income support
Ask the warehouse manager for a forklift job before robots arrive

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same message as before but less shouting, I hope. I'd say we have five years, so let's use them to set the rules now: who pays, who gets retrained, what happens to people like me. I'd want the union in the room with head office from year one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my job still goes, just in 2031 instead of 2028. Five years is enough to see it coming and not enough for someone like me to become someone else. At 48 I'd be young for a pension and old for starting over, which is a terrible place to stand when the computers come for buyers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use the first two years to pay down the credit card and build savings from four months to six or seven. I'd push the union for a deal where the company funds retraining, and I'd pick something with people in it, maybe the school catering side, because I know those kitchen managers. Leila and I would also tell the kids not to count on us paying much for university.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but less sick than the fast one. It's dread on a timer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd tell the kids not to count on help with university. What would you actually say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell our daughter Maya, who's nine, that she should pick something where you have to be in the room with people. Nursing like her mother, a trade, teaching little ones. I wouldn't tell her about the money until she's older.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Earlier you said you avoid new tools. With five years, would you learn the AI after all?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably have to, at least enough to supervise it. That's the part I keep pushing away. I'd rather spend the five years making sure there's a law that protects people than spend it learning to train my own replacement.

S3.say: I'd say we have five years, so let's set the rules now about who pays and who gets retrained. I'd want the union at the table with head office from the first year.
S3.think: My job still goes, just in 2031 instead of 2028. Five years is enough to see it coming but not enough for someone like me to become someone else.
S3.do: Pays off the credit card and builds savings from four months towards six or seven over two years. Pushes the union for company-funded retraining and eyes a move into the school catering side, where he knows the kitchen managers.
S3.feel: Dread on a timer: still anxious and alarmed, but less sick than in the fast picture.
S3.quote: At 48 I'd be young for a pension and old for starting over, which is a terrible place to stand when the computers come for buyers.
S3.fieldNote: Extra time moves David from panic to dread, but not to a plan he wants. He admits he would have to learn the AI to supervise it, then pushes the thought away in favour of a law. His children's futures are now where the worry lands.

steps.text: Pay off the credit card and grow savings to six months
Push the union for company-funded retraining for buyers
Ask about moving into the school catering accounts team

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly? Ten years is a gift, so let's not waste it arguing about whether thinking AI is real. Governments should be planning now for income support and retraining for whole industries. I'd say that at work and I'd vote on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be 53 when it hits, with maybe the mortgage nearly done. That's not great, but it's a different animal from the fast one. I could imagine getting through on a smaller job, if we plan properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd overpay the mortgage a bit each month so it's close to finished by 2036. I'd slowly take a course in food safety or catering management, something with kitchens and people, one evening a week. And I'd stay active in the union, because I think the deals you make early are the ones that hold.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy in the background, still anxious when I think about it properly. More like a bill due next year than one due today.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said a smaller job. What would that look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe running supplies for a hospital kitchen or a school group, where someone has to walk the storeroom and argue with the cook. Less money, sure. But if the mortgage is mostly paid, Leila and I can live on less.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you think the three-year gap between thinking AI and robots means in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It tells me to aim for the bits where hands and people count, but not to think hands are safe forever. By 2039 even the storeroom could have a robot in it. I'd be close to 56 then, and I'd just hope to be near the finish line.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is a gift and governments should plan income support and retraining now instead of arguing whether AI is real. I'd say it at work and vote on it.
S4.think: I'd be 53 when it hits, with the mortgage nearly done, which is a very different animal from the fast picture. I can imagine getting by on a smaller job if we plan.
S4.do: Overpays the mortgage each month to have it nearly finished by 2036. Takes an evening course in food safety or catering management and stays active in the union to lock in early deals.
S4.feel: Anxious when he thinks about it properly, though it feels like a bill due next year rather than today.
S4.quote: Ten years is a gift, so let's not waste it arguing about whether thinking AI is real.
S4.fieldNote: With a decade, David reaches for the mortgage and a modest move towards kitchens and people. He reads the robot lag sensibly: hands buy time, not safety. His union instinct persists across all three AGI pictures, while his personal adaptation stays small and slow.

steps.text: Overpay the mortgage monthly to clear most of it by 2036
Take an evening course in catering management
Stay active in the union to secure early job protections

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, no contest, because I'd have no time and no robot-proof corner of my job to hide in. What would help is a guarantee from government and the company together: your income is protected for a couple of years while you retrain, and it's paid for by the companies making money from this. Without that, a guy like me with four months saved just falls through the floor.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the growers. A computer will shop purely on price. If AI does the buying, small farms will lose the one person who rings them when the frost comes. Nobody counts that as a job loss, but it is one.

headlineQuote: If AI does the buying, small farms will lose the one person who rings them when the frost comes.
portrait: David Rahman, 43, buys fresh produce for Northgate Foods, a distributor supplying restaurants, care homes and school kitchens. He runs on phone calls, a nine-year-old spreadsheet and long ties with growers, and he openly avoids new tools. He stays calm if AI is hype but becomes anxious under steady change and panicked if AGI arrives in 2028, because nothing in his job needs hands and he has only about four months saved. His answer is collective: the union, letters to his MP and protections paid for by the companies, while personally he moves slowly towards kitchen and people-facing work. More time softens his fear without ever making him want to learn the technology.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries him most, because he'd have no time to prepare and no hands-on part of his job to fall back on.
whatWouldHelp: A guarantee from government and employers that his income is protected for a couple of years while he retrains, paid for by the companies profiting from AI.
